metadata.extraction_comment: Two independent developments: a rational discretised working-set approach (chapters 2-10) and a real-analytic epsilon-net approach (chapter 11), each with its own notion of worm (DP23 vs DP34).

nodes.name: Moser's worm problem
nodes.statement: \emph{Moser's worm problem} asks for the (convex) region of smallest area in the plane that contains a rotated and/or translated copy of every curve of unit length (a \emph{worm}). Any such region is called a \emph{Moser set}. The exact optimum is unknown; the best published upper and lower bounds sandwich it between $0.232239$ and $\pi/12$.
nodes.statement_short: Find the smallest-area (convex) planar region containing a rigid copy of every unit-length curve; the optimum is unknown.

nodes.name: Working set algorithm
nodes.statement: We create and iteratively mutate a \emph{working set} of convex candidate polygons satisfying the property that which any convex Moser set of size below $0.232240$ must contain a copy of at least one of the candidates. The working set is initialised with a single polygon, and then repeatedly mutated by replacing elements with collections of larger elements in ways that preserve the property, all the while removing any element of size greater than $0.232240$. If we can find a sequence of mutations that ends with an empty working set, we may conclude that no convex Moser set of area below $0.232240$ exists.
nodes.statement_short: Maintain a working set of convex candidate polygons that every small Moser set must contain; grow and prune it until it is empty.

nodes.name: Initialise
nodes.statement: The working set is initialised with a single polygon,
nodes.statement_short: Start with a single polygon.

nodes.name: Mutate
nodes.statement: and then repeatedly mutated by replacing elements with collections of larger elements in ways that preserve the property,
nodes.statement_short: Replace elements by collections of larger elements, preserving the invariant.

nodes.name: Remove large
nodes.statement: all the while removing any element of size greater than $0.232240$.
nodes.statement_short: Discard elements whose area exceeds the threshold.

nodes.name: Conclude on empty set
nodes.statement: If we can find a sequence of mutations that ends with an empty working set, we may conclude that no convex Moser set of area below $0.232240$ exists.
nodes.statement_short: An empty working set rules out small convex Moser sets.

nodes.name: Rational point
nodes.statement: A \emph{rational point} is an element of $\mathbb{Q}^2$, represented as a function $\mathrm{Fin}\,2 \to \mathbb{Q}$.
nodes.label: def:rational-point

nodes.name: Cross product, dot product, squared length
nodes.statement: For $u, v \in \mathbb{Q}^2$ we define $u \times v = u_0 v_1 - u_1 v_0$, $u \cdot v = u_0 v_0 + u_1 v_1$, and $\lVert v\rVert^2 = v_0^2 + v_1^2$.
nodes.label: def:rational-ops

nodes.name: Counterclockwise rotation by a right angle
nodes.statement: The map $R : (x, y) \mapsto (-y, x)$ is a $90^\circ$ counterclockwise rotation, and preserves squared length.
nodes.label: def:rotate90

nodes.name: Closed / open half-space
nodes.statement: A (closed, resp.\ open) \emph{half-space} is specified by a basepoint $b \in \mathbb{Q}^2$ and a nonzero inward normal $n \in \mathbb{Q}^2$; a point $p$ belongs to the half-space iff $n \cdot (p - b) \ge 0$ (resp.\ $> 0$).
nodes.statement_short: A half-space is given by a basepoint $b$ and nonzero inward normal $n$: points with $n\cdot(p-b)\ge 0$ (or $>0$).
nodes.label: def:halfspace

nodes.name: Half-space to the left of a directed edge
nodes.statement: Given distinct points $p_1, p_2 \in \mathbb{Q}^2$, the half-space strictly (resp.\ weakly) to the left of the directed segment $p_1 \to p_2$ uses basepoint $p_1$ and normal $R(p_2 - p_1)$.
nodes.definiendum: half-space to the left of $p_1 \to p_2$
nodes.label: def:toLeft

nodes.name: Lines and intersection
nodes.statement: A \emph{line} is a basepoint together with a nonzero direction vector. Two nonparallel lines have a unique intersection point, computed by Cramer's rule.
nodes.genus: basepoint together with a nonzero direction vector
nodes.label: def:line

nodes.name: Moving a half-space inward
nodes.statement: Given $d, \tau > 0$, one may translate the basepoint of a half-space inward along its normal by an amount in $[d, d+\tau]$, obtaining a new half-space contained in the original. The scaling factor is realised rationally via Lemma~\ref{lem:findRationalWithSquareBetween}.
nodes.statement_short: Translate a half-space's basepoint inward along its normal by an amount in $[d,d+\tau]$, using a rational scaling factor.
nodes.label: def:moveInward

nodes.name: Rational root with square between bounds
nodes.statement: Given $0 \le \ell < u$ in $\mathbb{Q}$, there is an explicit rational $r > 0$ with $\ell \le r^2 \le u$.
nodes.label: def:rational-utility

nodes.name: Correctness of findRationalWithSquareBetween
nodes.statement: The rational $r$ returned by \ref{def:rational-utility} satisfies $r > 0$, $\ell \le r^2$, and $r^2 \le u$.
assumptions: The rational $r$ returned by \ref{def:rational-utility}
conclusions: satisfies $r > 0$, $\ell \le r^2$, and $r^2 \le u$.
nodes.label: lem:findRationalWithSquareBetween

nodes.name: Non-degenerate polygon
nodes.statement: A \emph{non-degenerate polygon} is a tuple consisting of a natural number $n \ge 3$, a function $V : \mathrm{Fin}\,n \to \mathbb{Q}^2$ giving the vertices in counterclockwise order, and a proof that $V$ is injective.
differentia: a function $V : \mathrm{Fin}\,n \to \mathbb{Q}^2$ giving the vertices in counterclockwise order
nodes.label: def:nondegen-polygon

nodes.name: Convex polygon
nodes.statement: A \emph{convex polygon} is a non-degenerate polygon in which, for every directed edge $V_i \to V_{i+1}$, every other vertex lies strictly to the left of the edge. Strictness excludes collinear triples and therefore makes every vertex an extreme point of the convex hull of $\{V_i\}$.
differentia: for every directed edge $V_i \to V_{i+1}$, every other vertex lies strictly to the left of the edge
nodes.label: def:convex-polygon

nodes.name: Edges as half-spaces
nodes.statement: Each edge of a convex polygon defines a closed half-space weakly to its left; the polygon coincides with the intersection of these half-spaces.
nodes.label: def:toHalfSpaces

nodes.name: Containment and subset tests
nodes.statement: A point lies in a convex polygon iff it lies in every edge half-space. A convex polygon $P$ is a subset of $Q$ iff every vertex of $P$ lies in $Q$.
nodes.label: def:contains

nodes.name: Soundness of the containment test
nodes.statement: Any rational point accepted by the containment test of a convex polygon $Q$ lies in the real convex hull of $Q$'s vertices. Consequently, if the subset test accepts $(P, Q)$, then the real region of $P$ is contained in that of $Q$.

nodes.name: Proof of soundness of the containment test
nodes.statement: Fan triangulation from vertex $0$: by induction on the number of vertices, a point weakly to the left of every directed edge lies either in the hull of the first $n-1$ vertices (if it is weakly left of the closing diagonal) or in the last fan triangle, whose membership is witnessed by explicit barycentric coordinates (subtriangle areas over the total area). The fan triangles are positively oriented by the strict convexity invariant of the polygon.
nodes.statement_short: Fan triangulation from vertex 0 and induction on the number of vertices, with explicit barycentric coordinates.

nodes.name: Convex hull of a list of rational points
nodes.statement: The function \texttt{convexHullRationalPoints} returns, from a finite list of rational points, a list of extreme points in counterclockwise order starting at the lexicographically smallest point. \texttt{ConvexPolygon.ofList} upgrades this to an \texttt{Option ConvexPolygon}, returning \texttt{none} when fewer than three extreme points remain.
nodes.statement_short: convexHullRationalPoints returns the extreme points in counterclockwise order; ConvexPolygon.ofList returns none if fewer than three.
nodes.label: def:convexHullRationalPoints

nodes.name: Convex hull vertices are distinct
nodes.statement: The output of \texttt{convexHullRationalPoints} has no duplicates.
conclusions: The output of \texttt{convexHullRationalPoints} has no duplicates.
nodes.label: lem:convexHullRationalPoints-nodup

nodes.name: Intersection of half-spaces as a polygon
nodes.statement: Given a list of closed half-spaces, the convex polygon defined by their intersection is obtained by taking all pairwise boundary intersections and retaining those satisfying every half-space constraint.
output: the convex polygon defined by their intersection
nodes.statement_short: Intersect all pairs of boundary lines and keep the points satisfying every half-space constraint.
nodes.label: def:ofHalfSpaces

nodes.name: Pairwise intersections
nodes.statement: taking all pairwise boundary intersections
nodes.statement_short: Compute all pairwise intersections of the boundary lines.

nodes.name: Filter feasible points
nodes.statement: retaining those satisfying every half-space constraint.
nodes.statement_short: Keep only points satisfying all half-space constraints.

nodes.name: Shrinking a convex polygon
nodes.statement: Given $d, \tau > 0$, one shrinks a convex polygon by moving each edge inward by an amount in $[d, d + \tau]$ and intersecting the resulting half-spaces. The output is an \texttt{Option ConvexPolygon}, since the result may be empty.
nodes.statement_short: Move each edge inward by about $d$ and intersect the resulting half-spaces; the result may be empty.
nodes.label: def:shrink

nodes.name: Move edges inward
nodes.statement: moving each edge inward by an amount in $[d, d + \tau]$
nodes.statement_short: Translate every edge half-space inward by an amount in $[d,d+\tau]$.

nodes.name: Intersect
nodes.statement: intersecting the resulting half-spaces.
nodes.statement_short: Intersect the moved half-spaces.

nodes.name: Shoelace area
nodes.statement: The area of a convex polygon with vertex list $(V_0, \ldots, V_{n-1})$ is \[ \operatorname{area}(P) = \frac{1}{2} \left| \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (V_i)_0 (V_{i+1})_1 - (V_{i+1})_0 (V_i)_1 \right|. \]
nodes.label: def:shoelace

nodes.name: Area bridge
nodes.statement: The Lebesgue measure of the real convex hull of the vertices of a rational convex polygon equals its shoelace area.
assumptions: a rational convex polygon
conclusions: The Lebesgue measure of the real convex hull of the vertices of a rational convex polygon equals its shoelace area.
nodes.label: lem:area-bridge

nodes.name: Proof of the area bridge
nodes.statement: The hull decomposes into the fan triangles from vertex $0$: the fan covers the hull by the same induction as in Lemma~\ref{lem:contains-sound}, and the triangles overlap only in null diagonal segments. The separating diagonals are supplied by \emph{diagonal positivity} --- every vertex lies strictly left of every diagonal from vertex $0$ --- which follows from the edge conditions by transitivity of the angular order inside an open half-plane, an instance of the Grassmann--Pl\"ucker relation. Each fan triangle is the affine image of the standard simplex, whose volume $1/2$ is computed by reflecting it onto the other half of the unit square; the linear part scales by its determinant, the cross product of the edge vectors. Summing and telescoping the fan cross products yields the cyclic shoelace sum, which is nonnegative for a counterclockwise polygon.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose the hull into fan triangles from vertex 0, compute each triangle's area via an affine image of the standard simplex, and telescope to the shoelace sum.

nodes.name: Fan decomposition
nodes.statement: The hull decomposes into the fan triangles from vertex $0$: the fan covers the hull by the same induction as in Lemma~\ref{lem:contains-sound}, and the triangles overlap only in null diagonal segments.
nodes.statement_short: The hull is the union of fan triangles from vertex 0, overlapping in null sets.

nodes.name: Diagonal positivity
nodes.statement: The separating diagonals are supplied by \emph{diagonal positivity} --- every vertex lies strictly left of every diagonal from vertex $0$ --- which follows from the edge conditions by transitivity of the angular order inside an open half-plane, an instance of the Grassmann--Pl\"ucker relation.
nodes.statement_short: Diagonal positivity from the edge conditions via the Grassmann-Plucker relation.

nodes.name: Triangle area
nodes.statement: Each fan triangle is the affine image of the standard simplex, whose volume $1/2$ is computed by reflecting it onto the other half of the unit square; the linear part scales by its determinant, the cross product of the edge vectors.
nodes.statement_short: Each fan triangle's area is half the cross product of its edge vectors.

nodes.name: Telescope
nodes.statement: Summing and telescoping the fan cross products yields the cyclic shoelace sum, which is nonnegative for a counterclockwise polygon.
nodes.statement_short: Summing the fan cross products gives the shoelace sum.

nodes.name: Direct planar isometry
nodes.statement: A \emph{direct isometry} is a tuple $(c, s, t)$ with $c, s \in \mathbb{Q}$, $t \in \mathbb{Q}^2$, and $c^2 + s^2 = 1$. It acts on $p \in \mathbb{Q}^2$ by \[ \mathrm{apply}_{(c,s,t)}(p) = (c\,p_0 - s\,p_1,\; s\,p_0 + c\,p_1) + t. \]
nodes.label: def:direct-isometry

nodes.name: Direct isometries are bijections
nodes.statement: The action of a direct isometry on $\mathbb{Q}^2$ is both injective and surjective.
assumptions: a direct isometry
conclusions: is both injective and surjective.
nodes.label: lem:isometry-bijective

nodes.name: Applying an isometry to a polygon
nodes.statement: Applying a direct isometry vertex-wise to a convex polygon produces a convex polygon. Convexity is preserved because rotations preserve the cross products witnessing the ``strictly left of'' condition.
nodes.definiendum: applying a direct isometry to a convex polygon
nodes.label: def:applyPolygon

nodes.name: Composition of isometries
nodes.statement: Direct isometries are closed under composition, with $(c, s, t)_1 \circ (c, s, t)_2$ given by the usual product of rotation matrices and composed translation.
nodes.label: def:isometry-compose

nodes.name: Rational unit circle grid
nodes.statement: For each pair of naturals $(a, b) \ne (0, 0)$, the formulas $c = (a^2 - b^2)/(a^2 + b^2)$ and $s = 2ab/(a^2 + b^2)$ yield a rational point on the unit circle. Enumerating such pairs up to a resolution depending on a target \emph{maximum angle change} yields a finite rational grid on the unit circle.
nodes.statement_short: Rational points $((a^2-b^2)/(a^2+b^2), 2ab/(a^2+b^2))$ enumerated up to a resolution form a finite rational grid on the unit circle.
nodes.label: def:angleGrid

nodes.name: Angle grid lies on the unit circle
nodes.statement: Every $(c, s)$ produced by \texttt{angleGrid} satisfies $c^2 + s^2 = 1$.
assumptions: Every $(c, s)$ produced by \texttt{angleGrid}
conclusions: satisfies $c^2 + s^2 = 1$.
nodes.label: lem:angleGrid-spec

nodes.name: Isometry discretisation
nodes.statement: For a granularity $\epsilon > 0$, we form a finite list of direct isometries by pairing each angle from \texttt{angleGrid} with each translation on a rational grid intersected with the \texttt{LocationRange} (Definition~\ref{def:locationRange}). The angle resolution is scaled by the distance cutoff so that far-away points are still covered finely.
nodes.statement_short: Finite list of direct isometries: angles from angleGrid times translations on a rational grid within the location range.
nodes.label: def:discretizeIsometries

nodes.name: Area threshold
nodes.statement: The area threshold is $A_* := 232240 / 10^6 = 0.232240$. A Moser set with area strictly less than $A_*$ would improve the current best lower bound.
nodes.label: def:areaThreshold

nodes.name: Benchmark worms
nodes.statement: Three concrete convex polygons are fixed as benchmark worms: \begin{itemize} \item the isosceles right triangle with legs of length $1/2$, \item the unit square with side $1/3$, \item the right triangle with legs $1/3$ and $2/3$. \end{itemize} The \emph{initial worm} is taken to be the isosceles right triangle; by convention every candidate Moser set in the working set contains an un-shifted copy of it. Its area is exactly $1/8$.
nodes.statement_short: Three fixed convex polygons (two right triangles and a square); the initial worm is the isosceles right triangle with legs 1/2.
nodes.label: def:benchmark-worms

nodes.name: Location range and distance cutoff
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma := 4 A_*$. The \emph{location range} is the square $[-\sigma, \sigma]^2$, which upper-bounds the positions where a point of a working-set polygon may lie without already exceeding the area threshold (via a triangle formed with the initial worm). The \emph{distance cutoff} is $\sigma \cdot \overline{\sqrt{2}}$, where $\overline{\sqrt{2}} = 1414213562373095/10^{15}$ is a rational upper bound on $\sqrt 2$.
nodes.statement_short: The location range is $[-4A_*,4A_*]^2$; the distance cutoff is $4A_*$ times a rational upper bound for $\sqrt2$.
nodes.label: def:locationRange

nodes.name: Points outside the location range are excluded
nodes.statement: Any convex polygon containing the initial worm as well as a point outside the location range has area strictly greater than $A_*$. Concretely, if a rational point $p$ is not contained in the location range, then the convex hull of $\{p\}$ together with the vertices of the initial worm has area strictly greater than $A_*$.
assumptions: Any convex polygon containing the initial worm as well as a point outside the location range
if a rational point $p$ is not contained in the location range
conclusions: has area strictly greater than $A_*$.
the convex hull of $\{p\}$ together with the vertices of the initial worm has area strictly greater than $A_*$.
nodes.label: prop:locationRange-excludes

nodes.name: Proof that points outside the location range are excluded
nodes.statement: By definition the location range is the square with corners at $(\pm 4 A_*, \pm 4 A_*)$. If $p = (x, y)$ lies outside this square, then $\max(|x|, |y|) > 4 A_*$. The initial worm has vertices $(0,0)$, $(1/2, 0)$, $(0, 1/2)$, so the triangle formed by $p$ together with one of the legs of the initial worm (the leg of length $1/2$ along the axis where $p$ is far from the origin) has base $1/2$ and height greater than $4 A_*$, hence area greater than $A_*$. This triangle is contained in the convex hull of $p$ together with the worm vertices, so the hull's area exceeds $A_*$.
nodes.statement_short: A far point and a leg of the initial worm form a triangle of base 1/2 and height $>4A_*$, so area $>A_*$.

nodes.name: Coordinate bound
nodes.statement: By definition the location range is the square with corners at $(\pm 4 A_*, \pm 4 A_*)$. If $p = (x, y)$ lies outside this square, then $\max(|x|, |y|) > 4 A_*$.
nodes.statement_short: A point outside the square has a coordinate exceeding $4A_*$ in absolute value.

nodes.name: Triangle area
nodes.statement: The initial worm has vertices $(0,0)$, $(1/2, 0)$, $(0, 1/2)$, so the triangle formed by $p$ together with one of the legs of the initial worm (the leg of length $1/2$ along the axis where $p$ is far from the origin) has base $1/2$ and height greater than $4 A_*$, hence area greater than $A_*$.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle on a leg of the initial worm has area $>A_*$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: This triangle is contained in the convex hull of $p$ together with the worm vertices, so the hull's area exceeds $A_*$.
nodes.statement_short: The hull contains the triangle, so its area exceeds $A_*$.

nodes.name: Newton-style rational square root
nodes.statement: Given $s \ge 0$ and $\epsilon > 0$, the Newton iteration $x_{n+1} = (x_n + s/x_n)/2$ produces a rational $r$ with $|r - \sqrt{s}| < \epsilon$. Applied componentwise, this yields a rational approximation \texttt{distanceApprox} of the Euclidean distance between two rational points.
nodes.statement_short: Newton iteration gives a rational approximation of $\sqrt s$; applied to coordinates it approximates Euclidean distance (distanceApprox).
nodes.label: def:sqrtApprox

nodes.name: Newton iteration
nodes.statement: the Newton iteration $x_{n+1} = (x_n + s/x_n)/2$
nodes.statement_short: Iterate $x \mapsto (x+s/x)/2$.

nodes.name: Distance approximation
nodes.statement: Applied componentwise, this yields a rational approximation \texttt{distanceApprox} of the Euclidean distance between two rational points.
nodes.statement_short: Use it to approximate the distance between rational points.

nodes.name: Worm (rational polygonal path)
nodes.statement: A \emph{worm} is a polygonal path with at least two rational vertices. Its approximate total length is the sum of distance approximations along consecutive vertices, with per-segment error budget divided equally so the total error remains below a given $\epsilon$.
differentia: with at least two rational vertices
nodes.label: def:worm

nodes.name: Scaling a worm, unit worm
nodes.statement: A worm can be scaled by any rational factor; scaling by $1/\ell$ where $\ell$ is the approximate length brings the worm to approximately unit length. A \emph{unit worm} bundles a worm together with a uniform bound ensuring the approximate length tends to $1$ as $\epsilon \to 0$.
nodes.label: def:scaleToUnit

nodes.name: Convex hull of a worm
nodes.statement: The convex hull of a worm is a convex polygon (when the worm has at least three non-collinear vertices); it summarises all rigid motions of the worm that embed it into a convex target.
nodes.label: def:worm-hull

nodes.name: Moser set
nodes.statement: A set $M \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ is a \emph{Moser set} if for every worm $w$ of unit length there exists a direct isometry $\varphi$ with $\varphi(w) \subseteq M$.
differentia: for every worm $w$ of unit length there exists a direct isometry $\varphi$ with $\varphi(w) \subseteq M$
also_stated_at: Any such region is called a \emph{Moser set}.
nodes.label: def:moser-set

nodes.name: Approximate / computational Moser set
nodes.statement: Given a finite list of candidate worms $W$ and a finite list of isometries $I$, a set $M$ is a \emph{$(W, I)$-approximate Moser set} if for every $w \in W$ there exists $\varphi \in I$ with $\varphi(w) \subseteq M$.
nodes.label: def:approx-moser-set

nodes.name: Working set
nodes.statement: A \emph{working set} is a list of convex polygons. Intended invariants: \begin{enumerate} \item every polygon in the list contains a copy of the initial worm (Definition~\ref{def:benchmark-worms}) under some direct isometry; \item every Moser set of area strictly less than $A_*$ contains a copy of some polygon in the list under some direct isometry. \end{enumerate} Invariant 1 is currently a convention maintained by construction; Invariant 2 is the core correctness statement the algorithm preserves.
also_stated_at: The computational approach maintains a list of convex polygons, the \emph{working set}, with the invariant that every Moser set of area below the threshold contains (a rigid motion of) at least one polygon in the list.
nodes.statement_short: A list of convex polygons such that every Moser set of area below $A_*$ contains a copy of one of them (Invariant 2).
nodes.label: def:workingSet

nodes.name: Initial working set
nodes.statement: The initial working set contains exactly the initial worm.
nodes.label: def:initialWorkingSet

nodes.name: Minimum area
nodes.statement: The minimum area in a working set is the minimum of the shoelace areas of its polygons (taken as $0$ on the empty set).
nodes.label: def:minArea

nodes.name: Growable distance to the left of a vertex pair
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a convex polygon, $A_*$ a rational area threshold, and $V_i, V_j$ an ordered pair of (not necessarily adjacent) vertices of $P$. Let $\tau > 0$ be a rational tolerance. The \emph{growable distance to the left of the directed line $V_i \to V_j$} is a rational number $d \ge 0$ such that, writing $A_R$ for the area of $P$ lying weakly to the right of the directed line $V_i V_j$ and $T(d)$ for the area of the triangle formed by $V_i$, $V_j$, and a point at perpendicular distance $d$ to the left of the line, we have \[ A_R + T(d) \;\ge\; A_* , \] and $d$ is within the tolerance $\tau$ of the unique exact value for which equality holds.
nodes.statement_short: The distance $d$ to the left of line $V_iV_j$ at which the right-hand area plus triangle area reaches $A_*$, up to tolerance $\tau$.
nodes.label: def:growableDistance

nodes.name: Growth half-space to the left of a vertex pair
nodes.statement: Let $P$, $A_*$, $\tau$, and $V_i, V_j$ be as in Definition~\ref{def:growableDistance}, with growable distance $d$. The \emph{growth half-space} to the left of the pair $V_i, V_j$ is the closed half-space lying to the left of (and including) the line parallel to $V_i \to V_j$ at perpendicular distance $d$ on the left side of the directed line.
nodes.label: def:growthHalfspace

nodes.name: Threshold violated outside a growth half-space
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a convex polygon with rational vertices, $A_*$ a rational area threshold, $\tau > 0$ a rational tolerance, and $V_i, V_j$ an ordered pair of vertices of $P$. If a rational point $p$ lies strictly outside the growth half-space to the left of $V_i, V_j$ associated with $P$, $A_*$, and $\tau$, then the area of the convex hull of $P \cup \{p\}$ is strictly greater than $A_*$.
assumptions: Let $P$ be a convex polygon with rational vertices, $A_*$ a rational area threshold, $\tau > 0$ a rational tolerance, and $V_i, V_j$ an ordered pair of vertices of $P$.
If a rational point $p$ lies strictly outside the growth half-space to the left of $V_i, V_j$ associated with $P$, $A_*$, and $\tau$
conclusions: then the area of the convex hull of $P \cup \{p\}$ is strictly greater than $A_*$.
nodes.label: lem:threshold_violated_outside_growth_halfspace

nodes.name: Proof of threshold violation outside a growth half-space
nodes.statement: By the definition of the growth half-space, $p$ lying strictly outside means that the perpendicular signed distance from $p$ to the directed line $V_i V_j$, measured to the left, exceeds the growable distance $d$. The convex hull of $P$ together with $p$ contains both the portion of $P$ lying weakly to the right of the line $V_i V_j$ (of area $A_R$) and the triangle with vertices $V_i$, $V_j$, $p$, and these two regions intersect only along the segment $V_i V_j$, a set of measure zero. The triangle has base $|V_i V_j|$ and height equal to the left-distance from $p$ to the line, hence area strictly greater than $T(d)$. Therefore the hull's area is at least $A_R + T(\text{left-distance of } p) > A_R + T(d) \ge A_*$.
nodes.statement_short: The hull contains the part of $P$ right of $V_iV_j$ plus the triangle $V_iV_jp$, whose area exceeds $T(d)$.

nodes.name: Unfold definition
nodes.statement: By the definition of the growth half-space, $p$ lying strictly outside means that the perpendicular signed distance from $p$ to the directed line $V_i V_j$, measured to the left, exceeds the growable distance $d$.
nodes.statement_short: Outside the half-space means left-distance exceeds $d$.

nodes.name: Disjoint regions
nodes.statement: The convex hull of $P$ together with $p$ contains both the portion of $P$ lying weakly to the right of the line $V_i V_j$ (of area $A_R$) and the triangle with vertices $V_i$, $V_j$, $p$, and these two regions intersect only along the segment $V_i V_j$, a set of measure zero.
nodes.statement_short: Hull contains the right part of $P$ and the triangle, overlapping in a null set.

nodes.name: Triangle area
nodes.statement: The triangle has base $|V_i V_j|$ and height equal to the left-distance from $p$ to the line, hence area strictly greater than $T(d)$.
nodes.statement_short: The triangle has area $>T(d)$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore the hull's area is at least $A_R + T(\text{left-distance of } p) > A_R + T(d) \ge A_*$.
nodes.statement_short: Sum the areas to exceed $A_*$.

nodes.name: Growth half-space intersection polygon
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a convex polygon, $A_*$ a rational area threshold, and $\tau > 0$ a rational tolerance. The \emph{growth half-space intersection} associated to $P$, $A_*$, and $\tau$ is the intersection, over all ordered pairs $(V_i, V_j)$ of distinct vertices of $P$, of the growth half-spaces to the left of those pairs. Equivalently, it is the set of points $p$ such that for every ordered vertex pair $(V_i, V_j)$, the point $p$ lies in the growth half-space to the left of $V_i, V_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Intersection of the growth half-spaces over all ordered pairs of distinct vertices of $P$.
nodes.label: def:growthHalfspaceIntersection

nodes.name: Threshold violated outside the growth half-space intersection
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a convex polygon with rational vertices, $A_*$ a rational area threshold, and $\tau > 0$ a rational tolerance. If a rational point $p$ lies outside the growth half-space intersection of $P$, $A_*$, and $\tau$, then the area of the convex hull of $P \cup \{p\}$ is strictly greater than $A_*$.
assumptions: Let $P$ be a convex polygon with rational vertices, $A_*$ a rational area threshold, and $\tau > 0$ a rational tolerance.
If a rational point $p$ lies outside the growth half-space intersection of $P$, $A_*$, and $\tau$
conclusions: then the area of the convex hull of $P \cup \{p\}$ is strictly greater than $A_*$.
nodes.label: lem:threshold_violated_outside_growth_intersection

nodes.name: Proof of threshold violation outside the intersection
nodes.statement: If $p$ is outside the intersection, then there exists at least one ordered vertex pair $(V_i, V_j)$ such that $p$ lies strictly outside the growth half-space to the left of $(V_i, V_j)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:threshold_violated_outside_growth_halfspace}, the convex hull of $P \cup \{p\}$ then has area strictly greater than $A_*$.
nodes.statement_short: Some growth half-space excludes $p$; apply the single half-space lemma.

nodes.name: Big set removal
nodes.statement: Remove every polygon whose area strictly exceeds $A_*$. This preserves Invariant~2 because any Moser set of area below $A_*$ cannot have a polygon of strictly larger area as a subset.
nodes.statement_short: Drop every polygon of area above $A_*$.
nodes.label: def:bigSetRemoval

nodes.name: Big set removal preserves the working set invariant
nodes.statement: If a working set satisfies Invariant~2 of Definition~\ref{def:workingSet}, so does the result of big set removal.
assumptions: If a working set satisfies Invariant~2 of Definition~\ref{def:workingSet}
conclusions: so does the result of big set removal.
nodes.label: prop:bigSetRemoval-correct

nodes.name: Superset removal
nodes.statement: Process the polygons of the list sequentially, maintaining a list of retained polygons: a polygon $p$ is dropped when some already-retained polygon is a subset of $p$, and when $p$ is retained, any retained polygons having $p$ as a subset are dropped. A retained subset $q$ already witnesses Invariant~2 whenever $p$ does. (The sequential form matters: the vertex-containment test is not antisymmetric --- two distinct polygons, e.g.\ with cyclically rotated vertex lists, can each contain the other --- and the symmetric filter ``drop $p$ whenever some other $q \subseteq p$ is present'' would delete both members of such a pair, potentially removing the last witness of Invariant~3.)
nodes.statement_short: Sequentially keep polygons, dropping any polygon that contains an already-retained one and retained polygons that contain a new one.
nodes.label: def:supersetRemoval

nodes.name: Initialise retained list
nodes.statement: maintaining a list of retained polygons:
nodes.statement_short: Process polygons in order with a retained list.

nodes.name: Drop superset
nodes.statement: a polygon $p$ is dropped when some already-retained polygon is a subset of $p$,
nodes.statement_short: Drop $p$ if a retained polygon is a subset of it.

nodes.name: Prune retained
nodes.statement: and when $p$ is retained, any retained polygons having $p$ as a subset are dropped.
nodes.statement_short: On retaining $p$, drop retained polygons containing $p$.

nodes.name: Superset removal preserves the working set invariant
nodes.statement: If a working set satisfies Invariant~2, so does the result of superset removal.
assumptions: If a working set satisfies Invariant~2
conclusions: so does the result of superset removal.
nodes.label: prop:supersetRemoval-correct

nodes.name: Worm adding
nodes.statement: Given an additional worm presented as a convex hull, for each polygon $p$ in the current working set and for each isometry $\varphi$ in the discretisation, form the convex hull of $p$ together with the image under $\varphi$ of the \emph{shrunk} hull (to absorb discretisation error). The new working set collects all such unions. This step encodes the requirement that a Moser set must contain \emph{this} worm in some pose.
input: an additional worm presented as a convex hull
output: The new working set collects all such unions.
nodes.statement_short: For each polygon and each discretised isometry, take the hull of the polygon with the image of the shrunk worm hull.
nodes.label: def:wormAdding

nodes.name: Form unions
nodes.statement: for each polygon $p$ in the current working set and for each isometry $\varphi$ in the discretisation, form the convex hull of $p$ together with the image under $\varphi$ of the \emph{shrunk} hull (to absorb discretisation error).
nodes.statement_short: For each polygon and isometry, take the hull with the moved shrunk worm hull.

nodes.name: Collect
nodes.statement: The new working set collects all such unions.
nodes.statement_short: Return all these hulls as the new working set.

nodes.name: Worm adding preserves the working set invariant
nodes.statement: If the isometry discretisation is fine enough relative to the shrink amount, then adding a worm preserves Invariant~2 of Definition~\ref{def:workingSet}.
assumptions: If the isometry discretisation is fine enough relative to the shrink amount
conclusions: adding a worm preserves Invariant~2 of Definition~\ref{def:workingSet}.
nodes.label: prop:wormAdding-correct

nodes.name: Cleanup and combined add
nodes.statement: \texttt{cleanup} is the composition of big-set removal and superset removal. \texttt{addWormAndCleanup} adds a worm and then cleans up.
nodes.statement_short: cleanup = big-set removal then superset removal; addWormAndCleanup = worm adding then cleanup.
nodes.label: def:cleanup

nodes.name: Computational lower bound
nodes.statement: There exists a finite list of worms $W$ and a sequence of working-set updates that, starting from Definition~\ref{def:initialWorkingSet} and adding the worms in $W$ in turn using Definition~\ref{def:cleanup}, terminates with the empty working set. Consequently the area of every Moser set is at least $A_*$: \[ \inf \{ \operatorname{area}(M) : M \text{ is a Moser set}\} \ge A_*. \]
also_stated_at: This project pursues a \emph{computer-checked} improvement to the lower bound, by showing that every Moser set must contain a convex polygon of area at least $0.232240$.
nodes.statement_short: A finite worm list drives the working set to empty, so every Moser set has area at least $A_*=0.232240$.
conclusions: There exists a finite list of worms $W$ and a sequence of working-set updates that
terminates with the empty working set.
Consequently the area of every Moser set is at least $A_*$:
nodes.label: thm:lower-bound

nodes.name: Proof of the computational lower bound
nodes.statement: Any Moser set $M$ of area $<A_*$ must contain, in some pose, every polygon ever present in a working set produced by \texttt{addWormAndCleanup}, by Propositions \ref{prop:bigSetRemoval-correct}, \ref{prop:supersetRemoval-correct}, and \ref{prop:wormAdding-correct}. If the final working set is empty, this is a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Invariant preservation by the three propositions means a small Moser set contains a polygon of the final, empty working set: contradiction.

nodes.name: State of the Lean formalisation
nodes.statement: The Lean development does not assert Theorem~\ref{thm:lower-bound}; it proves the reduction \texttt{Moser.areaThreshold\_le\_moserCoverNumber\_of\_run}, which derives the bound from a certificate $\exists s,\ s.\mathtt{Sound} \wedge s.\mathtt{polygons} = []$. Two things are outstanding: that certificate (Proposition~\ref{prop:terminating-sequence}), and Proposition~\ref{prop:wormAdding-correct}, which is carried through the Lean statements as an explicit hypothesis \texttt{Moser.WorkingSet.WormAddingSound} rather than assumed silently. Every other statement in the development is proved; the file has no \texttt{sorry}.
nodes.statement_short: Lean proves the bound from a soundness certificate; the certificate and worm-adding soundness remain outstanding.
nodes.label: rem:lowerBoundLeanState

nodes.name: Terminating sequence of worms
nodes.statement: A finite list of worms ending the iteration with the empty working set can be found by computer search, e.g.\ starting from the benchmark worms of Definition~\ref{def:benchmark-worms} and augmenting with further worms arising from the enumeration scheme in \texttt{Moser.Worm.Enumeration} (currently stubbed).
conclusions: A finite list of worms ending the iteration with the empty working set can be found by computer search
nodes.label: prop:terminating-sequence

nodes.name: Worm (Lipschitz curve)
nodes.statement: A \emph{worm} is a $1$-Lipschitz curve $f : [0,1] \to \RR^2$.
nodes.label: def:lipschitz-worm

nodes.name: Pinned worm
nodes.statement: A worm $f$ is \emph{pinned} if $f(0) = (0,0)$. Since $f$ is $1$-Lipschitz on $[0,1]$, a pinned worm satisfies $\lvert f(x) \rvert \le x \le 1$ for all $x \in [0,1]$.
nodes.label: def:pinnedWorm

nodes.name: epsilon-thickening
nodes.statement: For a set $A \subseteq \RR^2$ and $\varepsilon \ge 0$, the \emph{$\varepsilon$-thickening} of $A$ is the closed $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood \[ A^{\varepsilon} \;=\; \{\, x \in \RR^2 : \dist(x, A) \le \varepsilon \,\}. \]
nodes.label: def:thickening

nodes.name: Grid polygonal worm
nodes.statement: Fix a step $\delta > 0$ and a vertex count $k \in \NN$. A \emph{$(k,\delta)$-grid polygonal worm} is a pinned worm obtained by choosing grid points $p_0, p_1, \dots, p_k \in \delta\ZZ \times \delta\ZZ$ with $p_0 = (0,0)$, setting $\tilde f(n/k) = p_n$ for $0 \le n \le k$, and interpolating linearly on each interval $[n/k, (n+1)/k]$, subject to the resulting curve being $1$-Lipschitz.
nodes.statement_short: Pinned piecewise-linear worm with $k+1$ nodes on the grid $\delta\mathbb Z^2$, required to be 1-Lipschitz.
nodes.label: def:gridPolygonalWorm

nodes.name: The node bound is automatic
nodes.statement: Requiring in addition that the nodes $p_0, \dots, p_k$ lie within distance $1$ of the origin does not change the set of $(k,\delta)$-grid polygonal worms. Indeed the interpolant is $1$-Lipschitz and pinned at the origin, so its whole range lies in the closed unit disc, and each node $p_n$ with $n \le k$ is a value of it: $p_n = \tilde f(n/k)$.
conclusions: Requiring in addition that the nodes $p_0, \dots, p_k$ lie within distance $1$ of the origin does not change the set of $(k,\delta)$-grid polygonal worms.
nodes.label: lem:gridNodesInDisc

nodes.name: epsilon-net of worms
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon > 0$. A set $S$ of worms is an \emph{$\varepsilon$-net of worms} if the image of every pinned worm is contained in the $\varepsilon$-thickening of the image of some element of $S$.
differentia: the image of every pinned worm is contained in the $\varepsilon$-thickening of the image of some element of $S$
nodes.label: def:epsilonNet

nodes.name: A finite grid epsilon-net exists
nodes.statement: \leanfile{Moser/Real/CompactnessOutline.lean} For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exist $k \in \NN$ and $\delta > 0$ such that the set $S_\varepsilon$ of all $(k,\delta)$-grid polygonal worms is finite and is an $\varepsilon$-net of worms.
assumptions: $\varepsilon > 0$
conclusions: there exist $k \in \NN$ and $\delta > 0$ such that the set $S_\varepsilon$ of all $(k,\delta)$-grid polygonal worms is finite and is an $\varepsilon$-net of worms.
nodes.label: thm:finiteEpsilonNet

nodes.name: Proof that a finite grid epsilon-net exists
nodes.statement: Choose $k > 2/\varepsilon$, so that $1/k < \varepsilon/2$, and then choose $\delta > 0$ small enough that $2\delta k + \delta < \varepsilon/2$. With these $k$ and $\delta$, the set $S_\varepsilon$ is finite: by Lemma~\ref{lem:gridNodesInDisc} the nodes lie in the closed unit disc, so each of the finitely many nodes ranges over the finitely many grid points of $\delta\ZZ \times \delta\ZZ$ there, and the nodes determine the worm. It remains to check that $S_\varepsilon$ is an $\varepsilon$-net. Fix a pinned worm $f$ and construct an element of $S_\varepsilon$ near it. Set \[ f_1 = \frac{1}{1 + 2\delta k}\, f , \] which is $\tfrac{1}{1+2\delta k}$-Lipschitz; since $f$ is pinned, $\lvert f(x) \rvert \le 1$, so \[ \lvert f(x) - f_1(x) \rvert = \lvert f(x) \rvert \cdot \frac{2\delta k}{1 + 2\delta k} \le 2\delta k . \] Let $\tilde f(n/k)$ be a nearest point of $\delta\ZZ \times \delta\ZZ$ to $f_1(n/k)$ for $0 \le n \le k$, and extend $\tilde f$ by linear interpolation. Each node moves by at most $\delta$ (half a grid cell in each coordinate), so on each subinterval of length $1/k$ the segment of $\tilde f$ has length at most $\tfrac{1}{k}\cdot\tfrac{1}{1+2\delta k} + 2\delta$; multiplying by $k$ shows the Lipschitz constant of $\tilde f$ is at most $\tfrac{1}{1+2\delta k}\,(1 + 2\delta k) = 1$, so $\tilde f$ is a $(k,\delta)$-grid polygonal worm, hence $\tilde f \in S_\varepsilon$. Comparing $f$ to $\tilde f$ at an arbitrary $x \in [0,1]$, the rescaling contributes at most $2\delta k$, the grid rounding at most $\delta$, and the linear interpolation at most $1/k$, so \[ \lvert f(x) - \tilde f(x) \rvert \;\le\; 2\delta k + \delta + \frac{1}{k} < \varepsilon . \] Therefore every point of the image of $f$ lies within $\varepsilon$ of the image of $\tilde f$, i.e.\ the image of $f$ is contained in the $\varepsilon$-thickening of the image of $\tilde f \in S_\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $k,\delta$ small; finiteness from the node bound. Rescale the worm, round its samples to the grid and interpolate: the result is a grid worm within $\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Choose parameters
nodes.statement: Choose $k > 2/\varepsilon$, so that $1/k < \varepsilon/2$, and then choose $\delta > 0$ small enough that $2\delta k + \delta < \varepsilon/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $k > 2/\varepsilon$ and small $\delta$.

nodes.name: Finiteness
nodes.statement: With these $k$ and $\delta$, the set $S_\varepsilon$ is finite: by Lemma~\ref{lem:gridNodesInDisc} the nodes lie in the closed unit disc, so each of the finitely many nodes ranges over the finitely many grid points of $\delta\ZZ \times \delta\ZZ$ there, and the nodes determine the worm.
nodes.statement_short: Nodes lie in the unit disc by the node-bound lemma, so finitely many grid worms.

nodes.name: Reduce to net property
nodes.statement: It remains to check that $S_\varepsilon$ is an $\varepsilon$-net.
nodes.statement_short: It remains to prove the net property.

nodes.name: Rescale
nodes.statement: Fix a pinned worm $f$ and construct an element of $S_\varepsilon$ near it. Set \[ f_1 = \frac{1}{1 + 2\delta k}\, f , \] which is $\tfrac{1}{1+2\delta k}$-Lipschitz; since $f$ is pinned, $\lvert f(x) \rvert \le 1$, so \[ \lvert f(x) - f_1(x) \rvert = \lvert f(x) \rvert \cdot \frac{2\delta k}{1 + 2\delta k} \le 2\delta k . \]
nodes.statement_short: Rescale $f$ to $f_1$, changing it by at most $2\delta k$.

nodes.name: Round to grid
nodes.statement: Let $\tilde f(n/k)$ be a nearest point of $\delta\ZZ \times \delta\ZZ$ to $f_1(n/k)$ for $0 \le n \le k$, and extend $\tilde f$ by linear interpolation. Each node moves by at most $\delta$ (half a grid cell in each coordinate), so on each subinterval of length $1/k$ the segment of $\tilde f$ has length at most $\tfrac{1}{k}\cdot\tfrac{1}{1+2\delta k} + 2\delta$; multiplying by $k$ shows the Lipschitz constant of $\tilde f$ is at most $\tfrac{1}{1+2\delta k}\,(1 + 2\delta k) = 1$, so $\tilde f$ is a $(k,\delta)$-grid polygonal worm, hence $\tilde f \in S_\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Round the samples to the grid; the interpolant is 1-Lipschitz, hence a grid worm.

nodes.name: Error estimate
nodes.statement: Comparing $f$ to $\tilde f$ at an arbitrary $x \in [0,1]$, the rescaling contributes at most $2\delta k$, the grid rounding at most $\delta$, and the linear interpolation at most $1/k$, so \[ \lvert f(x) - \tilde f(x) \rvert \;\le\; 2\delta k + \delta + \frac{1}{k} < \varepsilon . \]
nodes.statement_short: Total error $2\delta k + \delta + 1/k < \varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore every point of the image of $f$ lies within $\varepsilon$ of the image of $\tilde f$, i.e.\ the image of $f$ is contained in the $\varepsilon$-thickening of the image of $\tilde f \in S_\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Image of $f$ lies in the $\varepsilon$-thickening of a net element.

nodes.name: The enumeration of grid worms is complete
nodes.statement: \leanfile{Moser/Real/NetEnumeration.lean} Fix $k \ge 1$ and $c \ge 1$, and set $\delta = 1/(ck)$. A $(k,\delta)$-grid polygonal worm is determined by integer node data: a sequence of $k+1$ pairs in $\ZZ^2$ starting at $(0,0)$ whose consecutive steps have squared Euclidean norm at most $c^2$. The executable branching enumeration \texttt{netPaths} — start at the origin and repeatedly branch over the finitely many admissible steps — is \emph{complete}: every $(k,\delta)$-grid polygonal worm is traced by a generated path.
assumptions: Fix $k \ge 1$ and $c \ge 1$, and set $\delta = 1/(ck)$.
conclusions: every $(k,\delta)$-grid polygonal worm is traced by a generated path.
nodes.statement_short: With $\delta=1/(ck)$, the branching enumeration netPaths of integer node sequences with steps of norm at most $c$ covers every grid worm.
nodes.label: thm:netEnumeration

nodes.name: Proof of completeness of the grid-worm enumeration
nodes.statement: The nodes of a grid polygonal worm are consecutive samples of a $1$-Lipschitz curve at parameters $1/k$ apart, so consecutive nodes are at distance at most $1/k = c\delta$, i.e.\ their integer coordinates differ by an admissible step; the branching enumeration reaches every such sequence, and the piecewise-linear interpolant through the recovered nodes traces the same polyline.
nodes.statement_short: Consecutive nodes are at distance at most $c\delta$, i.e. admissible integer steps, so the branching enumeration reaches them.

nodes.name: Verified branch-and-bound epsilon-net
nodes.statement: \leanfile{Moser/Real/NetEnumeration.lean} The enumeration is followed by a greedy bound. Since a convex cover contains a worm iff it contains the worm's convex \emph{hull}, a path is redundant as soon as its hull is contained in an already-kept path's hull; the sweep \texttt{hullPrunedNetPaths} discards such paths, deciding hull coverage by an executable integer test (every node of the candidate lies in the hull of the keeper's nodes: point-on-segment by cross product and dot-product bounds, or point-in-triangle by common-sign cross products — complete in the plane by Carath\'eodory's theorem). For $k \ge 1$ and $c \ge 2$ the hulls of the surviving paths form an $\varepsilon$-net of worms with the explicit tolerance $\varepsilon = 2/c + 1/k + 1/(ck)$; in particular for every $\varepsilon > 0$, taking $k = c \ge \max(2, 4/\varepsilon)$ yields a finite, executably generated $\varepsilon$-net. For $c = 2$ the bound shrinks the $13, 169, 2197$ generated paths to $10, 65, 326$ for $k = 1, 2, 3$.
assumptions: For $k \ge 1$ and $c \ge 2$
conclusions: the hulls of the surviving paths form an $\varepsilon$-net of worms with the explicit tolerance $\varepsilon = 2/c + 1/k + 1/(ck)$
nodes.statement_short: Greedily pruning enumerated paths whose hull lies in a kept path's hull still yields an $\varepsilon$-net with $\varepsilon=2/c+1/k+1/(ck)$.
nodes.label: thm:hullPrunedNet

nodes.name: Proof of the verified branch-and-bound epsilon-net
nodes.statement: Soundness of the point-in-triangle test: the three cross products are the barycentric numerators of the query point, and when they share a sign with the (nonzero) triangle determinant, dividing by the determinant exhibits the point as an explicit convex combination of the three vertices; point-on-segment handles the degenerate collinear cases, and hull-in-hull follows by testing every node. The greedy sweep maintains the invariant that every generated path is covered by some kept path (a dropped path by the keeper that witnessed dropping it; a kept path by itself). For the net property: by the quantitative form of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:finiteEpsilonNet}, every pinned worm lies within $\varepsilon$ of some $(k,\delta)$-grid polygonal worm; by Theorem~\ref{thm:netEnumeration} that worm is the polyline of a generated path; the polyline lies inside its own hull, that hull is contained in a kept path's hull, and thickenings are monotone under set inclusion. The elements of the net are convex sets rather than worms, which the definition of an $\varepsilon$-net of worms permits.
nodes.statement_short: Soundness of the integer hull tests via barycentric numerators, a covering invariant for the greedy sweep, and the quantitative grid-net argument.

nodes.name: Test soundness
nodes.statement: Soundness of the point-in-triangle test: the three cross products are the barycentric numerators of the query point, and when they share a sign with the (nonzero) triangle determinant, dividing by the determinant exhibits the point as an explicit convex combination of the three vertices; point-on-segment handles the degenerate collinear cases, and hull-in-hull follows by testing every node.
nodes.statement_short: The cross-product tests exhibit explicit convex combinations.

nodes.name: Sweep invariant
nodes.statement: The greedy sweep maintains the invariant that every generated path is covered by some kept path (a dropped path by the keeper that witnessed dropping it; a kept path by itself).
nodes.statement_short: Every generated path stays covered by a kept path.

nodes.name: Net property
nodes.statement: For the net property: by the quantitative form of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:finiteEpsilonNet}, every pinned worm lies within $\varepsilon$ of some $(k,\delta)$-grid polygonal worm; by Theorem~\ref{thm:netEnumeration} that worm is the polyline of a generated path; the polyline lies inside its own hull, that hull is contained in a kept path's hull, and thickenings are monotone under set inclusion.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the grid-net theorem, enumeration completeness and hull monotonicity.

nodes.name: Net elements are hulls
nodes.statement: The elements of the net are convex sets rather than worms, which the definition of an $\varepsilon$-net of worms permits.
nodes.statement_short: Hulls as net elements are allowed by the definition.

nodes.name: The branch-and-bound worm search is sound
nodes.statement: \leanfile{Moser/Real/WormSearch.lean} The branch-and-bound search of the blog post references only the tolerance $\varepsilon$. A node consists of two point lists: points \emph{definitely in} the worm's convex hull and points \emph{definitely not in} it; the maybe region is implicit, so branching on a point $x$ is a pure dichotomy ($x$ is in the hull or it is not) and the search is exhaustive by construction. The search kills a branch when two included points are at distance $> 1$, or when the possible region lies in the $\varepsilon$-thickening of a net element (for $\varepsilon \ge 1$, a net element within $\varepsilon - 1$ of an included point suffices, since a worm hull has diameter at most $1$; in general the box $\bigcap_A (A + [-1,1]^2)$ over included points is used); it adopts the included points into the net when they escape all $\varepsilon/2$-thickenings; and both children of every branch are pruned by the redundancy rules: an included point in the hull of the other included points is dropped, and an excluded point $D$ is dropped when another excluded point $C$ lies in the hull of the included points together with $D$. If a fueled run closes every branch, the hulls of the collected net elements form an $\varepsilon$-net of worms — \emph{unconditionally}. For $\varepsilon \ge 1$ the run closes at the root with the singleton net $\{(0,0)\}$, checked at compile time; tolerances below $1$ await a coverage test that exploits the excluded points (the region avoids the shadow cone of every excluded point, a union of $2^{|\mathrm{excluded}|}$ convex pieces — the pruning is what keeps this exponent small). A strengthened length kill is specified but not yet implemented (\texttt{IsStrongLengthKill}): at slack $\varepsilon'$ it must pass every collection of included points containable in the hull of a length-$1$ worm and kill every collection not containable in a length-$(1+\varepsilon')$ worm; the gap between the thresholds is what makes the test finitely computable. Any conforming test slots into the search soundness unchanged (\texttt{IsStrongLengthKill.no\_consistent}), and the pairwise test satisfies the passing clause but not the killing clause (the vertices of a unit equilateral triangle are pairwise at distance $1$ yet need a worm of length at least $3/2$, by the half-perimeter lower bound). The kill side is implemented and verified (\texttt{tourCertCheck}, \texttt{strongLengthKill}): for any rational witnesses $w_1, w_2, w_3$ in the closed unit disc, probing with the directions $d_j = w_{j-1} - w_j$ forces one curve point beyond $M(d_j) = \max_{p \in I} \langle p, d_j\rangle$ each; doubling the worm bounds the three-stop tour by $2L$ — with three stops the tour length is visit-order independent, so no permutation analysis is needed — while Cauchy--Schwarz and a cyclic rearrangement bound it below by $\sum_j M(d_j)$. Thus $\sum_j M(d_j) > 2$, an exact rational check, kills soundly; witnesses along the edges of a spread triangle of included points recover the half-perimeter bound. The witness search is heuristic and carries no proof obligations. This strong kill is wired into the search. The passing clause also has a verified certificate (\texttt{passCheck}): a witness node list containing every included point whose $k$ consecutive gaps are each at most $(1+\varepsilon')/k$ — exact rational checks — yields a $(1+\varepsilon')$-Lipschitz piecewise-linear worm through the points (\texttt{passCheck\_sound}), with witnesses generated by greedy ordering and leg subdivision. What remains for a full \texttt{IsStrongLengthKill} instance is completeness: every collection is either killed by some tour certificate or passed by some witness.
assumptions: If a fueled run closes every branch
conclusions: the hulls of the collected net elements form an $\varepsilon$-net of worms
nodes.statement_short: If the in/out-point branch-and-bound search closes every branch, the collected hulls form an $\varepsilon$-net; kill and pass certificates are verified.
nodes.label: thm:bnbSearch

nodes.name: Proof of soundness of the worm search
nodes.statement: Soundness of the kill rules: two points of a worm hull are at distance at most $1$ (the worm has diameter at most $1$; passing to hulls twice through closed balls transports the bound); the ball rule serves a worm by the triangle inequality through the included point; the box rule serves it because every vertex of the box is within $\varepsilon$ of the net hull (exact rational nearest-point computations) and thickenings of convex sets are convex. The redundancy principles are verified semantically: were a dropped excluded point $D$ in the hull, convexity would force the witnessing excluded point $C$ in as well. Pruning only removes constraints, so it weakens nodes and preserves consistency. The run soundness is an induction over the fuel: every pinned worm consistent with a stack node, or already served, is served by the final net; the net only grows; branching preserves consistency by the hull-membership dichotomy; and every pinned worm is consistent with the root (the origin is in its hull).
nodes.statement_short: Each kill and redundancy rule is sound; run soundness by induction over the fuel. Key step: every pinned worm consistent with a stack node is served by the final net.

nodes.name: Kill rules sound
nodes.statement: Soundness of the kill rules: two points of a worm hull are at distance at most $1$ (the worm has diameter at most $1$; passing to hulls twice through closed balls transports the bound); the ball rule serves a worm by the triangle inequality through the included point; the box rule serves it because every vertex of the box is within $\varepsilon$ of the net hull (exact rational nearest-point computations) and thickenings of convex sets are convex.
nodes.statement_short: Distance, ball and box kills never discard a worm.

nodes.name: Redundancy sound
nodes.statement: The redundancy principles are verified semantically: were a dropped excluded point $D$ in the hull, convexity would force the witnessing excluded point $C$ in as well.
nodes.statement_short: Dropped points are implied by kept constraints.

nodes.name: Pruning preserves consistency
nodes.statement: Pruning only removes constraints, so it weakens nodes and preserves consistency.
nodes.statement_short: Pruning weakens nodes.

nodes.name: Induction on fuel
nodes.statement: The run soundness is an induction over the fuel: every pinned worm consistent with a stack node, or already served, is served by the final net; the net only grows; branching preserves consistency by the hull-membership dichotomy; and every pinned worm is consistent with the root (the origin is in its hull).
nodes.statement_short: Induct over the fuel: consistent worms are served by the final net.

nodes.name: Moser cover number
nodes.statement: A set $C \subseteq \RR^2$ is a \emph{cover} if for every worm $f$ there is an orientation-preserving isometry (a translation--rotation) $g$ of $\RR^2$ such that the image of $g \circ f$ is contained in $C$. The \emph{Moser cover number} $M$ is the infimum of $\area(C)$ over all convex covers $C$.
nodes.statement_short: A cover contains a rigid copy of every worm; the Moser cover number $M$ is the infimum area of convex covers.
nodes.label: def:moserNumber

nodes.name: Minimal convex cover of a finite set of worms
nodes.statement: For a finite set $S$ of worms, the \emph{minimal convex cover} $K(S)$ is a convex set of least area for which there exist translation--rotations $(g_s)_{s \in S}$ with the image of $g_s \circ s$ contained in $K(S)$ for every $s \in S$; that is, $K(S)$ minimises $\area\!\big(\conv \bigcup_{s \in S} g_s(\image\, s)\big)$ over all choices of translation--rotations $g_s$.
nodes.statement_short: $K(S)$ is a least-area convex set containing rigid placements of every worm in the finite set $S$.
nodes.label: def:minimalCover

nodes.name: Computability of the minimal convex cover
nodes.statement: The minimal convex cover $K(S)$ is the minimum, over all translation--rotations of the elements of $S$, of the area of the convex hull of their union. For a fixed finite $S$ this is a finite-dimensional optimisation problem in the placement parameters and is in principle computable, e.g.\ by quantifier elimination over the reals, and plausibly by convex optimisation.
nodes.statement_short: $K(S)$ is a finite-dimensional optimisation over placements, computable in principle by quantifier elimination.
nodes.label: rem:computeMinimalCover

nodes.name: Lower bound on the Moser number
nodes.statement: For any finite set $S$ of worms, $M \ge \area\big(K(S)\big)$.
assumptions: For any finite set $S$ of worms
conclusions: $M \ge \area\big(K(S)\big)$.
nodes.label: thm:lowerBound

nodes.name: Proof of the lower bound on the Moser number
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be any convex cover. Since every element of $S$ is a worm, for each $s \in S$ there is a translation--rotation $g_s$ placing $g_s \circ s$ inside $C$. Thus $C$ is a convex set admitting placements of all elements of $S$, so by minimality $\area(C) \ge \area(K(S))$. Taking the infimum over convex covers $C$ gives $M \ge \area(K(S))$.
nodes.statement_short: Every convex cover admits placements of all of $S$, so by minimality its area is at least that of $K(S)$; take the infimum.

nodes.name: Place worms in a cover
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be any convex cover. Since every element of $S$ is a worm, for each $s \in S$ there is a translation--rotation $g_s$ placing $g_s \circ s$ inside $C$.
nodes.statement_short: A convex cover $C$ admits placements of all worms of $S$.

nodes.name: Minimality
nodes.statement: Thus $C$ is a convex set admitting placements of all elements of $S$, so by minimality $\area(C) \ge \area(K(S))$.
nodes.statement_short: By minimality of $K(S)$, $\area(C)\ge\area(K(S))$.

nodes.name: Infimum
nodes.statement: Taking the infimum over convex covers $C$ gives $M \ge \area(K(S))$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the infimum over covers.

nodes.name: Upper bound on the Moser number
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and let $S_\varepsilon$ be a finite $\varepsilon$-net of worms. Then \[ M \le \area\!\big(K(S_\varepsilon)^{\varepsilon}\big), \] the area of the $\varepsilon$-thickening of the minimal convex cover of $S_\varepsilon$.
assumptions: Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and let $S_\varepsilon$ be a finite $\varepsilon$-net of worms.
conclusions: M \le \area\!\big(K(S_\varepsilon)^{\varepsilon}\big)
nodes.label: thm:upperBound

nodes.name: Proof of the upper bound on the Moser number
nodes.statement: Write $K = K(S_\varepsilon)$ with placements $(g_s)_{s \in S_\varepsilon}$. The $\varepsilon$-thickening $K^{\varepsilon}$ is convex. We claim it is a cover. Let $f$ be an arbitrary worm; after a translation--rotation we may assume $f$ is pinned. By Theorem~\ref{thm:finiteEpsilonNet} there is $s \in S_\varepsilon$ such that the image of $f$ is contained in the $\varepsilon$-thickening of the image of $s$. Applying the placement $g_s$, the image of $g_s \circ f$ is contained in the $\varepsilon$-thickening of the image of $g_s \circ s$, which lies in $K^{\varepsilon}$. Hence $K^{\varepsilon}$ is a convex cover, and $M \le \area(K^{\varepsilon})$.
nodes.statement_short: The $\varepsilon$-thickening of $K(S_\varepsilon)$ is a convex cover: each pinned worm is within $\varepsilon$ of a placed net element.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Write $K = K(S_\varepsilon)$ with placements $(g_s)_{s \in S_\varepsilon}$. The $\varepsilon$-thickening $K^{\varepsilon}$ is convex.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $K=K(S_\varepsilon)$ with placements; $K^\varepsilon$ is convex.

nodes.name: Thickening is a cover
nodes.statement: We claim it is a cover. Let $f$ be an arbitrary worm; after a translation--rotation we may assume $f$ is pinned. By Theorem~\ref{thm:finiteEpsilonNet} there is $s \in S_\varepsilon$ such that the image of $f$ is contained in the $\varepsilon$-thickening of the image of $s$. Applying the placement $g_s$, the image of $g_s \circ f$ is contained in the $\varepsilon$-thickening of the image of $g_s \circ s$, which lies in $K^{\varepsilon}$. Hence $K^{\varepsilon}$ is a convex cover, and $M \le \area(K^{\varepsilon})$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: $K^\varepsilon$ is a cover, hence $M \le \area(K^\varepsilon)$.

nodes.name: Nearby net element
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be an arbitrary worm; after a translation--rotation we may assume $f$ is pinned. By Theorem~\ref{thm:finiteEpsilonNet} there is $s \in S_\varepsilon$ such that the image of $f$ is contained in the $\varepsilon$-thickening of the image of $s$.
nodes.statement_short: Pin $f$ and pick a net element $s$ whose thickening contains it.

nodes.name: Apply placement
nodes.statement: Applying the placement $g_s$, the image of $g_s \circ f$ is contained in the $\varepsilon$-thickening of the image of $g_s \circ s$, which lies in $K^{\varepsilon}$.
nodes.statement_short: The placed worm lies in $K^\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence $K^{\varepsilon}$ is a convex cover, and $M \le \area(K^{\varepsilon})$.
nodes.statement_short: $K^\varepsilon$ is a convex cover, giving the bound.

nodes.name: Steiner gap, and what replaces it
nodes.statement: The natural way to control the gap between the bounds of Theorems~\ref{thm:lowerBound} and~\ref{thm:upperBound} is the planar Steiner formula: for a convex body $K$ with perimeter $L$ and every $\varepsilon \ge 0$, \[ \area\big(K^{\varepsilon}\big) = \area(K) + \varepsilon\, L + \pi \varepsilon^{2}. \] Mathlib has no Steiner formula (nor mixed volumes or intrinsic volumes), so the formalisation replaces it by the elementary dilation bound Theorem~\ref{thm:dilationBound}, which is weaker but suffices: it also makes the gap tend to $0$ with $\varepsilon$, and it needs no perimeter bound.
nodes.statement_short: The Steiner formula would control the gap between the bounds; lacking it in Mathlib, the formalisation uses the dilation bound.
nodes.label: rem:minkowskiSteinerGap

nodes.name: Planar Steiner formula
nodes.statement: The natural way to control the gap between the bounds of Theorems~\ref{thm:lowerBound} and~\ref{thm:upperBound} is the planar Steiner formula: for a convex body $K$ with perimeter $L$ and every $\varepsilon \ge 0$, \[ \area\big(K^{\varepsilon}\big) = \area(K) + \varepsilon\, L + \pi \varepsilon^{2}. \]
nodes.statement_short: For a convex body with perimeter $L$, the area of its $\varepsilon$-thickening is $\area(K)+\varepsilon L+\pi\varepsilon^2$.
assumptions: for a convex body $K$ with perimeter $L$ and every $\varepsilon \ge 0$
conclusions: \area\big(K^{\varepsilon}\big) = \area(K) + \varepsilon\, L + \pi \varepsilon^{2}.

nodes.name: Dilation bound
nodes.statement: Let $K \subseteq \RR^2$ be convex and suppose $K$ contains a disc of radius $r > 0$. Then for every $\varepsilon \ge 0$, \[ \area\big(K^{\varepsilon}\big) \le \Big(1 + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{r}\Big)^{2} \area(K). \]
assumptions: Let $K \subseteq \RR^2$ be convex and suppose $K$ contains a disc of radius $r > 0$.
for every $\varepsilon \ge 0$
conclusions: \area\big(K^{\varepsilon}\big) \le \Big(1 + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{r}\Big)^{2} \area(K).
nodes.label: thm:dilationBound

nodes.name: Proof of the dilation bound
nodes.statement: Passing to the closure changes neither side (the frontier of a convex set is null). A point at distance at most $\varepsilon$ from $K$ is of the form $x + b$ with $x \in K$ and $\lVert b\rVert \le \varepsilon$; writing $u = c + (r/\lVert b\rVert)\, b$ for the point of the disc in the direction of $b$, the point $x + b$ is the image under the homothety of centre $c$ and ratio $1 + \varepsilon/r$ of a convex combination of $x$ and $u$, hence of a point of $K$. The homothety multiplies area by $(1 + \varepsilon/r)^2$.
nodes.statement_short: The $\varepsilon$-thickening lies in the image of $K$ under the homothety of ratio $1+\varepsilon/r$ centred at the disc's centre.

nodes.name: Reduce to closed
nodes.statement: Passing to the closure changes neither side (the frontier of a convex set is null).
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $K$ is closed.

nodes.name: Homothety containment
nodes.statement: A point at distance at most $\varepsilon$ from $K$ is of the form $x + b$ with $x \in K$ and $\lVert b\rVert \le \varepsilon$; writing $u = c + (r/\lVert b\rVert)\, b$ for the point of the disc in the direction of $b$, the point $x + b$ is the image under the homothety of centre $c$ and ratio $1 + \varepsilon/r$ of a convex combination of $x$ and $u$, hence of a point of $K$.
nodes.statement_short: Each point of the thickening is a homothetic image of a point of $K$.

nodes.name: Area scaling
nodes.statement: The homothety multiplies area by $(1 + \varepsilon/r)^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Homothety scales area by $(1+\varepsilon/r)^2$.

nodes.name: A priori bound M <= pi/4
nodes.statement: $M \le \pi/4$.
conclusions: $M \le \pi/4$.
nodes.label: thm:apriori

nodes.name: Proof of the a priori bound
nodes.statement: A worm $f$ is $1$-Lipschitz on $[0,1]$, so every point of its image lies within $1/2$ of $f(1/2)$. Translating $f(1/2)$ to the origin places every worm inside the disc of radius $1/2$, which is convex; so that disc is a cover, of area $\pi/4$.
nodes.statement_short: Every worm lies within 1/2 of its midpoint, so the disc of radius 1/2 is a convex cover.

nodes.name: Every cover contains a disc of radius 1/20
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a family of worms containing the ``V worm'' $V$ --- the path from $(0,0)$ to $(1/2,0)$ to $(1/2,1/2)$ --- and let $K$ be a cover of $S$. Then $K$ contains a disc of radius $1/20$.
assumptions: Let $S$ be a family of worms containing the ``V worm'' $V$ --- the path from $(0,0)$ to $(1/2,0)$ to $(1/2,1/2)$ --- and let $K$ be a cover of $S$.
conclusions: $K$ contains a disc of radius $1/20$.
nodes.label: thm:coverDisc

nodes.name: Proof that every cover contains a disc of radius 1/20
nodes.statement: $K$ contains a placed copy of $V$, hence of the convex hull of $V$, the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1/2,0)$, $(1/2,1/2)$. That triangle contains the disc of radius $1/20$ centred at $(3/10, 1/10)$: the barycentric coordinates $1 - 2p_0$, $2p_0 - 2p_1$, $2p_1$ of a point $p$ of that disc are all nonnegative. Placements are isometries, so they carry discs to discs.
nodes.statement_short: A cover contains the hull of the V worm, a triangle containing an explicit disc of radius 1/20 (checked by barycentric coordinates).

nodes.name: Contains triangle
nodes.statement: $K$ contains a placed copy of $V$, hence of the convex hull of $V$, the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1/2,0)$, $(1/2,1/2)$.
nodes.statement_short: The cover contains a copy of the V worm's hull triangle.

nodes.name: Disc in triangle
nodes.statement: That triangle contains the disc of radius $1/20$ centred at $(3/10, 1/10)$: the barycentric coordinates $1 - 2p_0$, $2p_0 - 2p_1$, $2p_1$ of a point $p$ of that disc are all nonnegative.
nodes.statement_short: Barycentric coordinates show the disc of radius 1/20 lies in the triangle.

nodes.name: Transport disc
nodes.statement: Placements are isometries, so they carry discs to discs.
nodes.statement_short: Isometries carry discs to discs.

nodes.name: Approximating the Moser number
nodes.statement: For any target accuracy $x > 0$ there are a finite $\varepsilon$-net $S_\varepsilon$ of worms and a convex cover $K$ of it such that \[ \area(K(S_\varepsilon)) \le M \le \area(K^{\varepsilon}), \qquad \area(K^{\varepsilon}) - \area(K(S_\varepsilon)) \le x . \]
assumptions: For any target accuracy $x > 0$
conclusions: there are a finite $\varepsilon$-net $S_\varepsilon$ of worms and a convex cover $K$ of it such that
nodes.statement_short: For any $x>0$ there is a finite net whose lower and upper area bounds sandwich $M$ within $x$.
nodes.label: thm:approxAlgorithm

nodes.name: Proof of approximating the Moser number
nodes.statement: Take the grid $\varepsilon$-net of Theorem~\ref{thm:finiteEpsilonNet}, enlarged by the V worm, and let $K$ be a convex cover of it whose area exceeds $\area(K(S_\varepsilon))$ by at most $\eta$; such a $K$ exists because the convex hull of the placed copies realises the infimum up to $\eta$ (no Blaschke selection theorem is needed). By Theorem~\ref{thm:coverDisc}, $K$ contains a disc of radius $1/20$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:dilationBound} gives $\area(K^{\varepsilon}) \le (1 + 20\varepsilon)^2 \area(K)$. Since $\area(K) \le \area(K(S_\varepsilon)) + \eta \le \pi/4 + \eta$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:apriori}, the gap is at most $\big((1+20\varepsilon)^2 - 1\big)\pi/4 + (1+20\varepsilon)^2 \eta$, which is at most $x$ for $\varepsilon$ and $\eta$ chosen explicitly in terms of $x$.
nodes.statement_short: Grid net plus the V worm; its near-optimal cover contains a disc of radius 1/20, so the dilation bound and $M\le\pi/4$ control the gap.

nodes.name: Choose net and cover
nodes.statement: Take the grid $\varepsilon$-net of Theorem~\ref{thm:finiteEpsilonNet}, enlarged by the V worm, and let $K$ be a convex cover of it whose area exceeds $\area(K(S_\varepsilon))$ by at most $\eta$; such a $K$ exists because the convex hull of the placed copies realises the infimum up to $\eta$ (no Blaschke selection theorem is needed).
nodes.statement_short: Take the grid net with the V worm and a near-optimal convex cover $K$.

nodes.name: Dilation estimate
nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{thm:coverDisc}, $K$ contains a disc of radius $1/20$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:dilationBound} gives $\area(K^{\varepsilon}) \le (1 + 20\varepsilon)^2 \area(K)$.
nodes.statement_short: Disc of radius 1/20 plus the dilation bound bound $\area(K^\varepsilon)$.

nodes.name: Bound the gap
nodes.statement: Since $\area(K) \le \area(K(S_\varepsilon)) + \eta \le \pi/4 + \eta$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:apriori}, the gap is at most $\big((1+20\varepsilon)^2 - 1\big)\pi/4 + (1+20\varepsilon)^2 \eta$, which is at most $x$ for $\varepsilon$ and $\eta$ chosen explicitly in terms of $x$.
nodes.statement_short: Using $M\le\pi/4$ the gap is at most $x$ for suitable $\varepsilon,\eta$.

nodes.name: The bounds converge
nodes.statement: There are sequences $L_n \le M \le U_n$, each an area of an explicit convex cover of an explicit finite net of polygonal worms, with $U_n - L_n \to 0$.
conclusions: There are sequences $L_n \le M \le U_n$, each an area of an explicit convex cover of an explicit finite net of polygonal worms, with $U_n - L_n \to 0$.
nodes.label: cor:convergentBounds

nodes.name: Proof that the bounds converge
nodes.statement: Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:approxAlgorithm} with $x = 1/(n+1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the approximation theorem with $x=1/(n+1)$.

nodes.name: Polygonal approximation with m segments
nodes.statement: For every worm $w$ and every $m \ge 1$ there is a worm $w'$ made of $m$ segments with $w \subseteq (w')^{1/2m}$ and $w' \subseteq w^{1/2m}$; the same bounds hold for the convex hulls.
assumptions: For every worm $w$ and every $m \ge 1$
conclusions: there is a worm $w'$ made of $m$ segments with $w \subseteq (w')^{1/2m}$ and $w' \subseteq w^{1/2m}$; the same bounds hold for the convex hulls.
nodes.label: thm:polygonalApprox

nodes.name: Proof of polygonal approximation
nodes.statement: Sample $w$ at the parameters $j/m$ and join consecutive samples. Consecutive samples are at distance at most $1/m$, so the interpolant is $1$-Lipschitz; every parameter is within $1/2m$ of a sample, and every point of a segment is within $1/2m$ of one of its endpoints.
nodes.statement_short: Sample at $j/m$ and interpolate; Lipschitz bounds give the $1/2m$ closeness.

nodes.name: Pruning bound
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a worm and $0 \le a \le b \le 1$. If $f([a,b]) \subseteq A$ then the image of $f$ lies in the $\big(1 - (b-a)\big)$-thickening of $A$. In particular, if a set $P$ of points of the worm is traced on $[a,b]$ and $L$ is the minimal length of a $1$-Lipschitz curve covering $P$, then no point of the worm is further than $1 - L$ from $f([a,b])$.

nodes.name: Proof of the pruning bound
nodes.statement: A parameter outside $[a,b]$ is within $\max(a, 1-b) \le 1 - (b-a)$ of an endpoint of $[a,b]$, and $f$ is $1$-Lipschitz. The restriction of $f$ to $[a,b]$, reparametrised, is a $1$-Lipschitz curve of length $b - a$ covering $P$, so $L \le b - a$.
nodes.statement_short: Parameters outside $[a,b]$ are within $1-(b-a)$ of it and $f$ is 1-Lipschitz; the restriction covers $P$ so $L\le b-a$.
